html:
The Battle of Toulouse was fought in June 721, when Odo, duke of Aquitaine, broke a siege of the city by the Umayyad governor of al-Andalus, as-Samh ibn Malik al-Khawlani.

After taking Narbonne in 719, the Muslim rulers of al-Andalus pushed north into Septimania and Aquitaine. In 721 as-Samh besieged Toulouse. Odo, who ruled Aquitaine almost as an independent prince, brought a relief army. He hit the besiegers by surprise while they were occupied with the walls. As-Samh was killed and his army fled back toward Narbonne.

The victory made Odo's name across Christian Europe, and the pope sent his praise. It did not end the raids, which continued under later governors. In 732 Odo was beaten in the field near Bordeaux and asked his rival Charles Martel for help, which led to the Battle of Tours. Seen together, the two battles show that the Umayyad push into Gaul was checked more than once, and by different Christian leaders.
